pr_title: refactor(compiler): show meaningful diagnostic when reporting a template error fails
pr_body:
When the Angular compiler emits a diagnostic in a template file, it
forces TypeScript to parse that template. Templates are not TypeScript,
so this parse finds a bunch of parsing errors, which Angular then
ignores and we show the diagnostic anyways because we have more context.
This can lead to strange behavior in TypeScript because templates are so
weird that it can break the parser and crash the whole compiler.

For example, certain Angular templates can encounter failures fixed by
microsoft/TypeScript#45987, which are not easily debuggable and require
a TS upgrade to fix.

This commit introduces logic to handle the error gracefully, by falling
back to report the template error on the component class itself. The
diagnostic is extended to still reference the template location and
includes the failure's stack trace, to allow the parsing failure to be
reported to TypeScript (as parsing should in theory not cause a crash).

Closes #43970

---

@dgp1130 PTAL, curious to hear if you think this is sufficient or if you have suggestions to improve it.

issue_context.title: Show degraded errors when TypeScript fails to parse Angular templates
issue_context.body:
### Which @angular/* package(s) are relevant/releated to the feature request?

compiler-cli

### Description

As I understand it, when the Angular compiler emits a diagnostic in a template file, it forces TypeScript to parse that template. Templates are not TypeScript, so this parse finds a bunch of parsing errors, which Angular then ignores and we show the diagnostic anyways because we have more context. This can lead to strange behavior in TypeScript because templates are so weird that it can break the parser and crash the whole compiler.

For example, certain Angular templates can encounter failures fixed by https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/issues/45987, which are not easily debuggable and require a TS upgrade to fix.

### Proposed solution

We should update the compiler to catch any TS parsing failures and show a degraded version of the diagnostic, probably on the `@Component()` class. We know this will parse successfully and should be capable of showing the error. The diagnostic will be harder to communicate, since we can't show the offending line of code in the template, but we'll at least be able to give the error message and indicate that the message was degraded. We should also consider pointing users to file a bug, either against us or the TypeScript repository, since clearly something went very wrong to cause that degraded diagnostic.

### Alternatives considered

The TS parser should never crash _in theory_, it should always succeed just with some number of parsing errors encountered. Arguably the current situation is just fine and any failure from this are just a TypeScript bug. In practice however, Angular causes very strange code paths which always have the possibly to fall into a TS testing gap and break the compiler. The user pain is always real, and having even a less-useful Angular template error message is far better than a TS assertion error.

The one potential downside of the degraded diagnostic is that making this a less impactful failure means that users are less likely to report the breakage the root cause is less likely to be fixed. I think this should be a rare enough occurrence, that we don't need to be too concerned about that, but it is one aspect to keep in mind.

review_comments: Instead of this fake function with `set*()` and `reset*()` functions, could we just use Jasmine spies for that? It's effectively the same thing, but the test framework handles all the setup and restore functionality.

I am not sure how to achieve that nicely in this case, TBH. Spying on `ts.createSourceFile` is problematic in the sense that the test calls into that function multiple times, so we'd have to conditionally call through which I don't like. As for `parseTemplateAsSourceFile`, even if it becomes exported will Jasmine be able to spy on the ES export? That sounds sketchy to me.

> A failure occurred to report this error...

Sounds a bit awkward, maybe we could phrase it more actively like "Failed to report an error in..." I'm also wondering if we should say what failed or suggest the user file a bug against someone (us or TS). I'm not sure what we want users to do in this scenario beyond fixing their immediate bug.

I like `Failed to report an error in ...`, updated.

Your other point is indeed a good question. I wouldn't want to point people to TS directly, as I feel it's rather awkward for our users to report a TS bug with their Angular template as input source text. OTOH, reporting it to us isn't super actionable for us, but we'd likely be able to extract a minimum source file that causes the crash. I haven't updated the message for now, I'd be okay without a call to action if people see this.
SGTM, I don't feel too strongly about a call to action, I agree it's hard to get anything useful from this kind of error.
Should throw an actual `Error` object instead of a string.

That's what the previous test does, this one is particularly meant to throw a non-Error error. I'd be okay with removing this test in its entirety if you don't think that worth it, but I wanted to avoid potentially erroring while handling another error.

Ah sorry, didn't realize that was the point of the test. Since we don't own the code throwing the error, I agree it's worth being a little overprotective here. The TS team could always introduce a non-error throw and our code should tolerate that. I'm fine with leaving this as is.
